language.script_notes: Latin alphabet with distinctive Czech diacritics — the letters Ř, Ě and Ů/ů appear only in Czech, never in Slovak, so spotting any of them settles Czechia versus Slovakia at once. Guide signs use a layout without arrows, unlike the Slovak versions.

road_furniture.bollard_color: Black bollards with orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back; rarer blue and red variants exist. Only Slovakia uses the same design.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: Flat-fronted black post with reflective strips mounted on the black section.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: A wide 'type B' guardrail profile — angular with a central recess — used only in Czechia and Slovakia in Europe.
road_furniture.line_paint: Roads often have solid outer lines with no center line, which helps separate Czechia from Slovakia.
road_furniture.curb_style: Neat kerbs in towns; well-maintained road surfaces.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Wide, round concrete utility poles, often attached in pairs, with short metal crossbars holding the insulators and sometimes an upside-down-triangle pair of support bars. House numbers on a RED background with white text are the clearest Czechia tell. Signposts with a black cap on top also favour Czechia (not an absolute rule).

architecture.roof_style: Steep-pitched roofs on traditional houses; flat roofs on the many panel apartment blocks.
architecture.roof_material: Clay tile and slate widely used; corrugated metal and asphalt on utility buildings.
architecture.wall_construction: Prefabricated concrete panel apartment blocks (paneláky) — over a million flats were built between 1959 and 1995, and around a third of Czechs still live in them — now often renovated and painted in pastel colours; plastered masonry family houses in towns and villages; ornate Baroque, Gothic and Art Nouveau facades in historic centers such as Prague and Český Krumlov.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Pastel blues, pinks, yellows and greens on renovated paneláky; cream and warm-tinted plaster on older houses.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Pastel-painted panel apartment blocks; Baroque churches with onion-shaped spires; hilltop castles and chateaux; Prague's dense, ornate historic core.

nature.vegetation: Farmland and rolling countryside broken by beech, spruce and pine forest; hop fields and orchards in parts of Bohemia; vineyards in southern Moravia.
nature.terrain: A landlocked country of rolling hills and low mountains — the Bohemian basin is ringed by ranges such as the Krkonoše, Šumava and Ore Mountains, with the Moravian lowlands to the east.
nature.climate_signature: Temperate continental climate with cold winters and warm summers; often overcast and green.

vehicles.plate_color: White plate with black text and a blue EU strip on the left carrying 'CZ'.
vehicles.plate_format: Digit, letter code for the region, then digits (e.g. '1A2 3456'), where the first letters indicate the region of registration.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Škoda — Czech-made and headquartered in Mladá Boleslav — is by far the most common brand and a strong national tell.

google_coverage.coverage_notes: Dense, near-complete coverage of roads nationwide including small villages.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared bollard design, thin-B guardrails and paired round concrete poles from their common history
confusion_set.tiebreaker: House numbers on a red background with white text point to Czechia (Slovakia uses white with black lettering); the letters Ř, Ě and Ů appear only in Czech; Czech roads often have solid outer lines with no center line.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Central European architecture, Slavic languages, similar road furniture styles
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Poland's red-striped one-sided bollard and red-outlined yellow warning triangles are absent in Czechia, and Polish diacritics (ł, ż, ą, ę) differ from Czech ones (ř, ě, ů).

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared Central European architecture and terrain along the borders
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Czech-language signs, red house-number plates and the Czech black bollard with orange double reflectors differ from Austrian and German road furniture.
